# Post-Training: Adaptation and Alignment {#sec-post-training}

@sec-pretraining ended with a model that had read the web and could
not be spoken to. This chapter is about the second and third stages: the ones
that are comparatively cheap, that you can actually run, and that shape much of
the behaviour a user notices. What the model knows and can do still comes
largely from pretraining and the architecture.

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain why a base model answers a question with another question, and what
  supervised fine-tuning changes so that it stops;
- write a training example in chat-template form and say which tokens the loss
  is computed on and why the rest are masked;
- work out, from a model's `config.json`, how many parameters a LoRA adapter
  on given target matrices adds, and estimate the run's GPU memory once you
  state your precision, batch, sequence-length and training-setup assumptions;
- distinguish SFT, RLHF, DPO, and GRPO by the data, the reward signal and the
  training compute each one needs;
- choose between prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning, and distillation with an
  explicit decision rule;
- look for catastrophic forgetting by evaluating the model before and after on
  general tasks and held-out benchmarks chosen before training.

## The model that answers a different question {#sec-base-model-failure}

Here is the problem in one representative exchange (the actual output varies
with the model, the prompt and the sampling settings). You have a base model —
the raw output of stage 1, nothing else done to it. You type:

```text
What is the capital of Turkey?
```

and it may continue:

```text
What is the capital of France?
What is the capital of Germany?
What is the largest city in Turkey?
```

Nothing has gone wrong. [The model did exactly what it was trained to do, and
that is the problem]{.hl}. It was trained on one objective — *given this text,
what text usually comes next* — and reading the prompt as the start of a list
of questions is a reading that objective allows. It may be completing a
worksheet; with another prompt or sampling setting it may just say "Ankara".
Supervised fine-tuning aims to make the question-and-answer behaviour
*reliable*.

::: {.column-margin}
Try this yourself: on the Hub, models named `Llama-3.1-8B` and
`Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct` are the same pretraining run. The first is the base
model. The second has been through the two stages in this chapter. The
difference in behaviour is large; the post-training compute for these two
models is not published. For scale, a separate example: the SFT (4.9) and
PPO-ptx (60) figures reported for InstructGPT's 175B version total 64.9
petaflop/s-days against 3,640 for GPT-3's pretraining — about 1.8%, or a factor
of 56, leaving out the reward model and data collection.
:::

Give the same base model a fact it very likely knows, phrased as a sentence to
be finished — `The capital of Turkey is` — and it may well produce "Ankara".
That shows it can use the fact in some contexts, not that it will answer every
question correctly and consistently. What is missing here is less information
than a *convention*: that a question addressed to you is a request for an
answer from you.

This is worth being precise about, because it sets up everything that follows.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Four things you might be missing, and what to try first for each.**

| what is missing | symptom | what to try first |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **knowledge** | confidently wrong about your documents, your prices, last week | retrieve the source and verify the answer (@sec-rag) |
| **format** | right content, wrong shape: prose where you needed JSON | a clear prompt, constrained decoding or an output schema |
| **behaviour** | answers the wrong *kind* of question; wrong register; inconsistent refusals | evaluate with examples; fine-tune if needed (this chapter) |
| **cost** | accurate enough, but too slow or too expensive per call | a smaller model, quantization or distillation |

These are not strict mappings (retrieval fails if it fetches the wrong
document, and knowledge can also be added by continued pretraining), but they
are a good start. Fine-tuning a model whose knowledge is out of date on
behaviour examples alone may not fix the problem if the problem is a wrong
source.
:::

We will come back to that table at the end and turn it into a decision tree.
First, the machinery.

**What we will look at.** First the training example and loss mask of
supervised fine-tuning, then LoRA and preference optimization; after that,
feedback that is not human, distillation and continued pretraining. Finally,
when *not* to fine-tune, and how to measure performance regressions after you
adapt a model.

## What the stages actually do {#sec-stage-anatomy}

@sec-pretraining drew the three stages by scale. Here is the same
pipeline drawn by *mechanism*: what each stage puts in, what signal it
optimizes, and which weights it is allowed to touch.

::: {.fig-cap}
The column that matters is the third one. Pretraining scores *what came next in
the corpus*; SFT scores *what should come next in the answer* (usually on the
assistant's tokens only); the preference-tuning example shown scores *which of
two answers is better*. That last signal cannot be written down as a single
target string — which is why it needs different algorithms. Other
post-training methods can use a verifiable reward or a chosen response text
instead; which fits depends on the data you have.
:::
::::

Notice what stages 2 and 3 have in common: neither one is where the model's
knowledge of the world mostly comes from. That is not a claim that supervised
fine-tuning *cannot* teach facts — it demonstrably can, and continued
pretraining on domain text is a standard way to add some. The claim is about
scale and reliability: a stage-2 run touching a few million tokens should not
be expected to revise, broadly and dependably, a world model built from
millions of times more text (15.6 trillion tokens against a few million).
Chosen examples can change some factual answers, but whether the change lasts
and generalises to other questions has to be tested separately. [When people
reach for fine-tuning as their knowledge-update mechanism, it often
disappoints]{.hl}. For information that changes often or needs a citable
source, retrieval is usually the better place to start; @sec-rag covers
it.

## Supervised fine-tuning {#sec-sft}

### One example, in full

A [supervised fine-tuning](#gloss-supervised-fine-tuning){#term-supervised-fine-tuning .term-ref}
example is usually one or more user messages and the assistant response you
wish the model had given; below we use a single-turn one. The idea is simple.
Most of the difficulty is in the details of how it is written down, and two of
those details can break runs silently.

::: {#gloss-supervised-fine-tuning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**supervised fine-tuning** — training on example messages and target
responses with the ordinary next-token loss. In this chapter's setup the loss
is computed on the assistant response alone; other setups target other
positions too. The same objective as pretraining; a different choice of which
text it is applied to.
[↩](#term-supervised-fine-tuning){.term-back}
:::

Here is a single Turkish example as it exists in a JSONL file (in JSONL each example is one line):

```text
{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? 'Kargo çok hızlı geldi, teşekkürler.'"}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "Olumlu."}]}
```

Before the model sees it, that structure is flattened into a single token
sequence by the model's [chat template](#gloss-chat-template){#term-chat-template .term-ref} — a
string template that in most distributions ships with the tokenizer
configuration and differs between model families; training and serving should
use the template that matches the model version:

::: {#gloss-chat-template .column-margin .term-gloss}
**chat template** — the exact string format, with roles, message boundaries
and special marker tokens, that turns a conversation into model input. In most
distributions it ships with the tokenizer configuration, and using the wrong
one usually degrades quality quietly rather than raising an error.
[↩](#term-chat-template){.term-back}
:::

```text
<|begin_of_text|><|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>

Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? 'Kargo çok hızlı geldi, teşekkürler.'<|eot_id|><|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>

Olumlu.<|eot_id|>
```

Those `<|...|>` markers are special tokens with their own embeddings in this
model family's tokenizer, and they mark the boundary between the user's message
and the assistant's turn. The behaviour of *answering* rather than continuing
is learned from training on examples formatted with them: mechanically, the
model learning what should follow the assistant header.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Do not hand-write the template; check its output.** Call
`tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)` on a training example
and print the result; check that the role markers and the response boundary are
where you expect. Model families use different markers, and a template mismatch
between training and serving usually degrades quality with no error message
anywhere — quietly enough that people can spend weeks blaming the data. It is
one of the common ways an otherwise correct-looking fine-tune underperforms.

At inference, if the template expects a separate assistant header, call it
with `add_generation_prompt=True`: that appends the empty assistant header,
which is the model's cue that it is now its turn to answer (training examples
do not get it, since the answer is already there). Forget it and even a
well-tuned chat model may simply continue the user's message; check the
sequence it produces.
:::

### Loss masking: the detail that silently breaks runs

Now the second detail. With Llama 3's tokenizer the sequence above is 31 tokens
long (re-run), and four of them are the answer: `Ol`, `umlu`, `.` and
`<|eot_id|>`. On which tokens do you compute the loss?

If you say *all of them* — which is what you get if you naively reuse the
pretraining objective — then most of the loss terms, 27 positions, teach the
model **to generate the prompt and the template**. Those terms do not have
equal-sized gradients, but the target is no longer just the answer: you are
pushing the model to model the user's text as well. For answer-focused SFT,
masking the non-assistant target positions is the more direct choice.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Loss masking: which tokens the gradient is allowed to come from</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 268" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="Two rows of token boxes over the same sequence. The top row, labelled wrong, shades every token including the user prompt, with a note saying twenty-seven of thirty-one loss terms teach the model to write the prompt and template. The bottom row, labelled right, shades only the four assistant response tokens and greys the rest, with a note saying only the response contributes to the loss. Both rows show the same token sequence: a header marker, the Turkish question, an assistant header marker, the word Olumlu, and an end-of-turn marker.">
  <text x="14" y="22" class="t-xs t-b t-muted">THE SAME 31-TOKEN SEQUENCE, TWO CHOICES OF LOSS MASK</text>

  <text x="14" y="60" class="t-xs t-b t-rose">✗ loss on everything</text>
  <rect x="14" y="72" width="120" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="74" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">user header</text>
  <rect x="140" y="72" width="330" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="305" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? …</text>
  <rect x="476" y="72" width="136" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="544" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">assistant header</text>
  <rect x="618" y="72" width="76" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="656" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">Olumlu.</text>
  <rect x="700" y="72" width="50" height="30" rx="5" class="box-rose"/>
  <text x="725" y="92" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono">eot</text>
  <text x="14" y="122" class="t-xs t-rose">27 of 31 loss terms teach the model to write the question and template.</text>

  <text x="14" y="168" class="t-xs t-b t-accent">✓ loss on the response only</text>
  <rect x="14" y="180" width="120" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="74" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-muted">user header</text>
  <rect x="140" y="180" width="330" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="305" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-muted">Bu yorum olumlu mu olumsuz mu? …</text>
  <rect x="476" y="180" width="136" height="30" rx="5" class="box"/>
  <text x="544" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-muted">assistant header</text>
  <rect x="618" y="180" width="76" height="30" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="656" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-b">Olumlu.</text>
  <rect x="700" y="180" width="50" height="30" rx="5" class="box-accent"/>
  <text x="725" y="200" class="t-xs t-mid t-mono t-b">eot</text>
  <text x="14" y="230" class="t-xs t-muted">Masked tokens are still read — they are the context. They just do not enter the loss.</text>
  <text x="14" y="252" class="t-xs t-b">Set the label of every masked position to −100 and the loss function skips it.</text>
</svg>
```
::: {.fig-cap}
Masking is not about hiding the prompt from the model. The user's message stays
in the input and the model still attends to every prompt token; that is what
the response being *conditioned* on it means. The mask only decides which
next-token predictions enter the loss: the target labels of the user message
and template markers are `-100`, those of the assistant response are token
ids.
:::
::::

In practice you build a `labels` tensor that is a copy of `input_ids` with
every non-response position set to `-100`, the default `ignore_index` of
PyTorch's cross-entropy loss, which then *ignores* those positions. Modern SFT libraries do this for you if you tell them
where the response starts; the failure mode is reaching for a plain causal-LM
training loop and forgetting. Two related details. If your model or trainer
shifts the loss internally, do not shift the labels yourself: Hugging Face
causal-LM models already compare the prediction at position $t$ with the label
at $t+1$, and shifting twice trains the model to predict two tokens ahead.
Check the alignment on a small example. And in a multi-turn conversation the
common choice is to keep the loss on *every* assistant turn and mask every user
turn, not just the last exchange; choose which turns to target for your task.

::: {.column-margin}
There is one legitimate reason to train on prompt tokens: if your prompts are
themselves in a domain the base model has never seen, the extra signal helps
the model learn the language of that domain. It is a deliberate choice, and it should be
justified in your run notes rather than inherited from a copied script.
:::

### How many examples do you actually need?

The honest answer is that the field's own numbers span three orders of
magnitude. They are figures reported by different projects with different aims,
data types and quality bars — not a common scale of need — but the spread
itself is informative.

| project | reported SFT input | what they were for |
|:--|--:|:--|
| LIMA [@zhou2023lima] | 1,000 | showing that a *little* is enough |
| InstructGPT [@ouyang2022training] | 12,725 prompts | a general-purpose assistant |
| Self-Instruct [@wang2023selfinstruct] | ~52,000 instructions | synthetic data; only 175 human-written seed tasks |
| Tülu 3 [@lambert2025tulu3] | 939,344 prompts | a competitive open recipe |

That last row hides the real work. Tülu 3's team assembled **23,327,961**
candidate prompts and kept 939,344 of them for supervised fine-tuning — under
one in twenty-four — with a further 425,145 routed to preference tuning
[@lambert2025tulu3]. The published artefact is a filtering decision far more
than it is a collection effort.

LIMA is the interesting entry. Its authors fine-tuned a 65B LLaMa on exactly
1,000 curated prompt-response pairs — 750 harvested from community Q&A sites
(Stack Exchange, wikiHow, Reddit), 250 written or adapted by the authors — with *no* reinforcement learning and *no*
preference modelling at all. Against GPT-4, human raters judged LIMA's answers
equal or better 43% of the time; against Bard 58%, against the RLHF-trained
DaVinci003 65% [@zhou2023lima].

There is a second reason a small set can go so far, shown in 2021 by the FLAN
work, before LIMA: a model fine-tuned on a *collection* of instruction-phrased tasks improves on
tasks it never saw during that fine-tune [@wei2022finetuned]. What SFT installs
is not a list of answers but the habit of treating an instruction as one.

To explain their own experiments, the LIMA authors propose what they call the
**Superficial Alignment Hypothesis**: essentially all of a model's knowledge
and capability is acquired during pretraining, and alignment mainly teaches it
*which sub-distribution of formats to use* when interacting with users. If that
is right, a thousand good examples can be enough to specify a format. The
hypothesis does not mean that fine-tuning can teach no facts, or that a
thousand examples suffice for every task; you have to measure on yours.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The practical reading.** Start with a small, clean set that represents your
target inputs and run a baseline; then measure the gain on a separate
validation set as you add examples. As a rough intuition: in small sets added
examples still buy format, as the set grows they buy coverage of the *variety*
of inputs, and larger still they buy robustness on the long tail. When the gain
flattens, choose between collecting more, fixing labels, covering rare cases
and widening the evaluation; the marginal *hour of quality control* is often
worth more than the marginal example.

LIMA and Tülu 3 are examples, at two very different scales, of data selection
shaping the result: in both, curation mattered as much as collection.
:::

## Parameter-efficient tuning {#sec-lora}

Everything so far assumed you can run the training step at all. As models
grow, a full training step soon stops fitting on the single GPU you are likely
to have. The limit is set by the optimizer state, the activations, the sequence
and batch length and the GPU memory as much as by model size: in the example
setup below, 1B parameters need about 16 GB for parameter-related state alone,
before activations. Most of that is not the weights themselves but the extra
state that training them brings.

### Where the memory actually goes

Count the bytes one parameter costs during mixed-precision AdamW training in
a common *example setup* — bf16 compute weights and gradients, an fp32 master
copy and two fp32 Adam moments. Check which copies your implementation actually
keeps, and the activations and temporary buffers, separately. Other configurations exist and cost
differently: 8-bit optimizer states, fused fp32-free schemes and sharded
optimizers all change this table. The 16 is a default, not a law.

| what is stored | bytes per parameter | why it exists |
|:--|--:|:--|
| bf16 weight | 2 | the model itself |
| bf16 gradient | 2 | one per **trainable** parameter |
| fp32 master weight | 4 | bf16 has too few mantissa bits to accumulate tiny updates |
| fp32 Adam $m$ | 4 | running mean of the gradient |
| fp32 Adam $v$ | 4 | running mean of the gradient *squared* |
| **total, trainable** | **16** | |
| **total, frozen** | **2** | a weight you never update only has to be read |

::: {.column-margin}
The fp32 master copy is the least obvious row and the one people try to delete
first. Without it, an update of size $10^{-5}$ added to a weight of size $1$
rounds straight back to $1$ in bf16 — while fp32 keeps it, as 1.00001 — and the
training silently stalls. Pick the example carefully: $10^{-8}$ would vanish in
fp32 as well, since single precision has about seven decimal digits. In this setup
it is the fp32 master copy that accumulates the small updates. That does not
make an fp32 copy mandatory for every low-precision run: other optimizer and
update schemes solve the problem differently, and then the memory arithmetic
changes too.
:::

Read the two totals against each other. [In this example setup the model
itself is one eighth of the parameter bill. The fp32 rows — the master copy and
Adam's two moments — are three quarters of it, and the gradient is the
remaining eighth.]{.hl} That ratio is where
[parameter-efficient fine-tuning](#gloss-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning){#term-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning .term-ref}
(PEFT) gets its saving on parameter state: freeze a parameter and *seven* of
its eight instalments disappear, leaving only the bf16 weight you still have to
read. Activations and compute remain; do not carry this saving over to total
GPU memory as a factor of 8 (the lab in @sec-lora-lab measured 1.40×).

::: {#gloss-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning .column-margin .term-gloss}
**parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)** — the family LoRA belongs to: train
a small fraction of the weights (or a few added ones) and leave the rest
frozen. Usually written *PEFT*.
[↩](#term-parameter-efficient-fine-tuning){.term-back}
:::

The arithmetic is checkable against a published figure. QLoRA states that
16-bit fine-tuning of a 65B LLaMA "requires more than 780 GB of GPU memory"
[@dettmers2023qlora]. One example calculation that explains its size:

$$
65 \times 10^9 \;\text{params} \times 12 \;\text{bytes} = 780 \;\text{GB}
$$

Twelve bytes per parameter — and the paper does not itemise its memory, so
this product is a possible decomposition, not the paper's own. One reading
against the table above is the three fp32 rows, master weight, $m$ and $v$;
in the 16-byte setup the bf16 weight and gradient bring parameter-related state
to $65 \times 16 = 1{,}040$ GB, before activations and buffers, consistent with
"more than". A second reading fits the same twelve exactly: bf16 weight, bf16
gradient, fp32 $m$, fp32 $v$, no master copy, with "more than" absorbing
activations instead. [In either reading most of the headline number is state
that exists only because the parameter is being trained.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
Reconstructing a published memory figure is worth doing precisely because it
usually has more than one solution. Papers report totals, not itemisations; you
infer the itemisation from the total, and honesty requires saying which one you
assumed.
:::

The LoRA paper's figure moves in the other direction: on GPT-3 175B, training
VRAM falls "from 1.2TB to 350GB" [@hu2022lora]. The endpoint is clean —

$$
175 \times 10^9 \times 2\;\text{bytes} = 350\;\text{GB}
$$

is the raw size of the frozen bf16 weights. The starting point is less clean.
1.2 TB across 175B parameters is about 6.9 bytes each, well under the 16 the
table predicts, so that figure was measured under a setup the paper does not
spell out. Either cheaper per-parameter state (8-bit or 16-bit optimizer
moments, no fp32 master copy) or keeping part of the state off the GPU (CPU
offloading, for instance) could explain it; the paper does not say which.
Sharding across many cards and activation checkpointing do not explain it on
their own: sharding spreads the same bytes over more GPUs, and checkpointing
trims activations, not the per-parameter state. The 350 GB, too, matches the
raw size of the frozen bf16 weights; the adapter and activations also take
room, so the equality does not account for every item in the paper. Quote both
figures as *their* report: you can recompute what the 350 GB corresponds to,
but you cannot recover the 1.2 TB's itemisation from the two totals.

### The low-rank hypothesis

So we want to freeze the weights. But a frozen model does not learn. The
question is what you can add on the side that is small enough to be cheap and
expressive enough to be useful.

[LoRA](#gloss-lora){#term-lora .term-ref}'s answer starts from an assumption about what fine-tuning does. A
pretrained weight matrix $W_0$ is a general-purpose feature map, built from a
very wide range of text. The change you need for *one* task can plausibly be
much narrower. The hypothesis [@hu2022lora] is that this adjustment
$\Delta W$, while it is a full $d \times k$ matrix in shape, can be
approximated well enough by a low-rank product — it has **low intrinsic
rank**. That is not a guarantee that the full fine-tuning update is low-rank
in every task and every layer; it is a constraint LoRA finds useful.

If that is true, you can write it as a product of two thin matrices:

$$
W_0 + \Delta W = W_0 + BA, \qquad B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r},\; A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}, \qquad r \ll \min(d,k)
$$

::: {#gloss-lora .column-margin .term-gloss}
**LoRA** — low-rank adaptation: freezing a pretrained weight matrix and
learning a small pair of matrices whose product is added to it. The pair has
$r(d+k)$ parameters instead of $dk$. In a compatible serving setup the update
can be folded back into the original weight, removing the extra matrix
multiply; measure the latency of an unmerged or quantized model separately.
[↩](#term-lora){.term-back}
:::

Count what that saves. For one of Llama 3.1 8B's $4096 \times 4096$ query
projections, $\Delta W$ in full has $16{,}777{,}216$ parameters. At $r = 8$,
$BA$ has $8 \times (4096 + 4096) = 65{,}536$ — **256 times fewer**, for the
same output shape.

### What $A$ and $B$ actually hold

The two matrices are not symmetric in role, and the asymmetry is the part
worth understanding.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}

The left path passes through the frozen pretrained matrix W-zero of shape d by k, drawn as a large solid block labelled frozen, sixteen point eight million parameters. The right path passes first through matrix A of shape r by k, described as choosing which r directions of the input this task cares about, then through matrix B of shape d by r, described as deciding what to write into the output for each of those directions. The right path is scaled by alpha over r and the two paths are summed. ```
::: {.fig-cap}
Follow the detour from $x$ to $h$: $A$ projects the input down to an
$r$-dimensional space, and $B$ projects those $r$ numbers back up to the output
size. On an intuitive reading $A$ picks *which few directions of the input*
are used and $B$ *what to write into the output* from them. But that is a
reading of the computation; we cannot give the learned $A$ and $B$ a unique
meaning each, because different factor pairs give the same product: for any
invertible $R$, $(BR^{-1})(RA) = BA$.
:::
::::

The initialisation, too, makes sense once you ask what happens otherwise. For
$h = W_0x + BAx$, $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial B$ is proportional to $Ax$
and $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A$ to $B$ (given a non-zero upstream loss
gradient):

| $A$ init | $B$ init | what happens |
|:--|:--|:--|
| zero | zero | $BA = 0$ and both gradients are zero: gradient descent cannot move the pair off zero |
| random | random | $BA$ is generally $\neq 0$ at step 0, so training *starts* by changing the pretrained model |
| **random** | **zero** | $BA = 0$ at step 0, $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial B$ generally $\neq 0$: the run starts exactly at the pretrained model and $B$ moves first |
| zero | random | also $BA = 0$ at step 0, $\partial \mathcal{L} / \partial A$ generally $\neq 0$: also escapes zero, with $A$ moving first |

Two of the four work, not one. Both of the bottom rows start the adapted model
exactly at the pretrained model *and* have somewhere to go, because the
gradient with respect to each matrix is proportional to the *other* one — so
you only need one of the pair to be non-zero. [For the starting output, what
matters is the product, not which factor carries the randomness.]{.hl} The
training trajectory need not be the same for the two choices: gradient and
optimizer dynamics can differ.

LoRA takes the third row: "a random Gaussian initialization for $A$ and zero
for $B$" [@hu2022lora]. The paper states the convention and does not argue for
it over the fourth row, and neither will this book. What the $B = 0$
initialisation buys is that the adapter leaves the pretrained model untouched at
step 0: you start from a model that already works, where random–random
initialisation would start the run away from the pretrained model.

### Rank and alpha, and why there are two knobs

The update is not added raw. It is scaled by $\alpha / r$, where $\alpha$ is a
constant you choose [@hu2022lora]:

$$
h = W_0 x + \frac{\alpha}{r} B A x
$$

The stated purpose of the division is practical rather than theoretical. The
authors write that the scaling "helps to reduce the need to retune
hyperparameters when we vary $r$" [@hu2022lora] — the aim is to stop a rank
sweep from silently becoming a learning-rate sweep at the same time. That does
not mean gradient size or the best learning rate stays the same across ranks
(@kalajdzievski2023rank shows that under $1/r$ scaling gradients shrink at
high rank); do the rank sweep on validation data.

$\alpha$ is a fixed multiplier on the whole adapter path, and the paper says
how it sees it: "tuning $\alpha$ is *roughly* the same as tuning the learning
rate" [@hu2022lora]. Roughly: $\alpha$ scales the adapter's contribution in
the forward pass and interacts with the learning rate without being identical
to it; its best value has to be judged together with the learning rate, the
rank and the target modules. The widespread convention $\alpha = 2r$ means, in
the forward pass, "scale the adapter by 2".

That convention is the community's, not the authors'. They report setting
$\alpha$ "to the first $r$ we try" and then leaving it alone. In other words,
they did not tune it. Note also that this is *not* $\alpha = r$ at every rank:
if you fix $\alpha$ at 8 because you tried $r = 8$ first, then $r = 16$ runs
at $\alpha/r = 0.5$. [Treat $\alpha = 2r$ as a default someone else picked for you, not
as a result.]{.hl}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Two knobs, two questions; tune both by measuring.**

- **$r$** sets the adapter's parameter count and the rank the update may have:
  *how much capacity does this adaptation need?* When the task is far from
  pretraining (a new language, a new notation), a higher rank is worth trying.
- **$\alpha/r$** scales the adapter's contribution: *how hard should the
  adapter push?*

Underfitting or confident nonsense can come not only from rank or alpha but
from the data, the learning rate, the number of epochs and the target modules.
Try a small rank/scale grid at fixed data and learning rate, and judge the
results both on task performance and on regression against the starting model.
They are commonly conflated because $\alpha = 2r$ makes them move together;
break the convention when you sweep.
:::

### The arithmetic of an adapter

A LoRA adapter on a $d_{\text{in}} \times d_{\text{out}}$ matrix adds exactly
$r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})$ *adapter parameters*. Everything else is
bookkeeping: which matrices you attach to, and how many layers there are. The
total trainable count can also include biases, a classification head or other
modules left trainable; the table below counts adapters only (the lab table
adds the head).

The three configurations below were computed from each model's own
`config.json` (we recomputed every row):

| model | targets | $r$ | trainable | share of model |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| BERTurk base (110.6M, 12 layers) | query, value | 8 | 294,912 | 0.267% |
| | + key, output | 8 | 589,824 | 0.533% |
| | + the MLP | 8 | 1,327,104 | 1.200% |
| Llama 3.1 8B (32 layers, $d$=4096) | q_proj, v_proj | 8 | 3,407,872 | 0.042% |
| | all attention | 8 | 6,815,744 | 0.085% |
| | attention + MLP | 8 | 20,971,520 | 0.261% |
| Qwen 2.5 7B (28 layers, $d$=3584) | q_proj, v_proj | 8 | 2,523,136 | 0.033% |
| | attention + MLP | 8 | 20,185,088 | 0.265% |

::: {.column-margin}
LoRA is not the only parameter-efficient method; it is one of the most widely
used today. Prompt tuning [@lester2021power] trains the representations of a
handful of *virtual tokens* prepended to the input and leaves the base model's
weights untouched; in its authors' experiments it becomes competitive with full
fine-tuning as the model grows. The memory, quality and latency trade-offs of
these methods vary with model size and task.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
Qwen's `q_proj, v_proj` adapters come to 2.52M against Llama's 3.41M, and it is
tempting to credit grouped-query attention (@sec-attention-cost) — Qwen 2.5 7B
uses 4 key-value heads to Llama's 8, making `v_proj` a $3584 \times 512$ matrix
rather than $4096 \times 1024$. Give Qwen 8 KV heads and the count rises to
2.64M, so GQA is only about 13% of the 884,736-parameter gap. The rest is
$d = 3584$ against 4096, over 28 layers against 32.
:::

Two things fall out. First, adding the MLP matrices to an attention adapter is
the largest jump on the table: 2.25× on BERTurk, 3.08× on Llama (from
`q_proj, v_proj` alone, 4.5× on BERTurk, 6.2× on Llama, 8.0× on Qwen). The jump
comes from the number and size of the target matrices; separately, the MLP
does hold much of these models' weights (by our count ~70% of Llama 3.1 8B,
~75% of Qwen 2.5 7B, ~51% of BERTurk). Second, even the most generous setting
here is under 0.3% of an 8B model. Raising $r$ from 1 to 128 multiplies the
adapter count on the same targets by 128 — no one should expect quality to
rise in proportion — yet even the top of that range stays well under one
percent of the model:

| $r$ | 1 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 | 64 | 128 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| trainable (q,v only) | 425,984 | 1.70M | 3.41M | 6.82M | 13.6M | 27.3M | 54.5M |
| share of Llama 3.1 8B | 0.005% | 0.021% | 0.042% | 0.085% | 0.170% | 0.340% | 0.679% |

Even at $r = 128$ you are training two thirds of one percent of the model.

### Work out your own run

The arithmetic above is for one configuration. Yours will differ, and the
numbers move faster than intuition does — so rather than trusting a rule of
thumb, put your own model size and rank in. The widget gives an **approximate
subtotal of weights, gradients and optimizer state** for the parameter count
and storage scheme you choose; the GPU memory a run needs also depends on
activations, sequence and batch length, temporary buffers and the
implementation. Do not use the result as a guarantee that a run fits.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof loraN = Inputs.range([0.1, 405], { value: 8.03, step: 0.01, label: "Model size (billions of parameters)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof loraShare = Inputs.range([0.005, 5], { value: 0.52, step: 0.005, label: "Adapter size (% of model)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof loraMode = Inputs.select(
  ["full fine-tune", "LoRA (bf16 base)", "QLoRA (4-bit base)"],
  { value: "LoRA (bf16 base)", label: "Method" }
)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
loraCalc = {
  const N = loraN * 1e9;
  const trainable = loraMode === "full fine-tune" ? N : N * loraShare / 100;
  const frozen = N - trainable;
  const baseBytes = loraMode.startsWith("QLoRA") ? 0.5 : 2; // QLoRA: raw 4-bit weights only, a lower bound (no scaling constants)
  const bytes = frozen * baseBytes + trainable * 16;
  const gib = bytes / 2 ** 30;
  const cards = [16, 24, 40, 48, 80, 141];
  const fits = cards.find((g) => gib * 1.35 < g); // an assumed 35% headroom, not a real fit test
  return { trainable, gib, fits, full: (N * 16) / 2 ** 30 };
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse; font-size:0.95rem">
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">trainable parameters</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        loraCalc.trainable >= 1e9
          ? (loraCalc.trainable / 1e9).toFixed(2) + "B"
          : (loraCalc.trainable / 1e6).toFixed(1) + "M"
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">weights + gradients + optimizer</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${loraCalc.gib.toFixed(1)} GiB</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">first card with an assumed 35% headroom (not a fit guarantee)</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        loraCalc.fits ? loraCalc.fits + " GB" : "none of the listed cards"
      }</td></tr>
  <tr><td style="padding:6px 10px">versus a full fine-tune</td>
      <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right; font-weight:600">${
        (loraCalc.full / loraCalc.gib).toFixed(1)
      }× less</td></tr>
</table>
<p style="font-size:0.85rem; opacity:0.75; margin-top:8px">
Activations and activation gradients are excluded, and at LoRA-sized adapter
counts they are not a rounding error — see the caution below. The "card"
column allows 35% headroom for them, which is a convention chosen for this
widget, not a measured constant. The QLoRA row counts raw 4-bit weights only;
quantization scaling constants and unquantized layers are left out.</p>`
```

The defaults are Llama 3.1 8B (8.03B parameters) with an $r{=}16$ adapter on
attention and MLP — 41,943,040 parameters, or 0.52% of the model. The
widget's *static-state-only* sums: full fine-tune **119.7 GiB**, past every
common 24–80 GB single-GPU configuration; LoRA on a bf16 base **15.5 GiB**;
QLoRA on a raw 4-bit base **4.3 GiB**. Without activations, temporary buffers
and QLoRA's scaling metadata you cannot say which card they fit; the caution
below shows why that matters.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**What this widget leaves out is the part that will surprise you.** It counts
weights, gradients and optimizer state, because those are what LoRA removes.
It does not count activations, and once the optimizer is gone they are what is
left. QLoRA's authors measured it: for a 7B LLaMA at batch size 1, with an
adapter at "commonly used 0.2% of the original model weights", the LoRA *input
gradients* occupy 567 MB while the LoRA *parameters* occupy 26 MB; with
gradient checkpointing the first figure drops to an average of 18 MB per
sequence [@dettmers2023qlora]. [In that example the LoRA input gradients take
about twenty-two times the room of the adapter you are training.]{.hl} Those
values belong to that model, batch size and sequence length; they do not carry
over to another setup.

This is why gradient checkpointing appears in common LoRA recipes, and why the
widget's numbers are a subtotal rather than an estimate. Before choosing a
card, run a short pilot on the target setup and measure peak memory. It is also why
the lab at the end of this chapter measures a much less dramatic ratio than the
arithmetic here predicts.
:::

### QLoRA: quantize the part you are not training

That last step needs one more idea. In the LoRA row above, the 15.5 GiB static
subtotal is now almost entirely the frozen bf16 base — the adapter's optimizer state is a
rounding error. So squeeze the base.

QLoRA [@dettmers2023qlora] does exactly that, storing frozen weights in a
4-bit format called **NF4** and dequantizing each block back to bf16 only for
the moment it is needed in the forward and backward pass. Three pieces make it
work:

- **4-bit NormalFloat**, a data type whose 16 levels are placed at the
  quantiles of a normal distribution — chosen because trained network weights
  are close to normally distributed, so the levels land where the weights
  actually are;
- **double quantization**, which quantizes the per-block scaling constants
  themselves, because at small block sizes those constants become a
  non-trivial share of the total;
- **paged optimizers**, which, on supported unified-memory setups, let
  optimizer state spill to CPU memory during memory spikes and so manage some
  of them; the gain and the speed cost have to be measured on the
  implementation.

The headline result: fine-tuning a 65B model goes from ">780 GB of GPU memory
to &lt;48 GB without degrading the runtime or predictive performance compared to
a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline" [@dettmers2023qlora] — a result reported for
the paper's own task comparisons. Their Guanaco 65B, trained this way in 24
hours on a single GPU, reached 99.3% of ChatGPT's score on the 80-question
Vicuna benchmark, as scored by GPT-4 acting as judge rather than by humans;
that ratio is not a general accuracy or human-preference measure (on the limits
of LLM judges see @sec-llm-eval-judge).

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**"Without degrading" is measured against full fine-tuning, not plain LoRA.**
The paper's claim covers runtime too, but its comparison is a 16-bit *full*
fine-tune. Against plain LoRA, dequantizing blocks on every forward and
backward pass costs arithmetic; on the other hand, lower memory use can ease
other bottlenecks in some setups. QLoRA buys you the ability to run at all on a
small card; on a card where plain LoRA already fits, measure the step time of
both on the same hardware and batch.
:::

### The payoff nobody mentions until they are on call

LoRA has an operational property that matters more, in a company, than any of
the training savings: an adapter can be **merged back into the base weights**.
Since $h = W_0x + \frac{\alpha}{r}BAx = (W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA)x$, you can
compute that sum once, in a suitable linear layer, and ship an ordinary model;
the separate adapter multiply goes away — the paper's "no additional inference
latency" [@hu2022lora]. Real latency still depends on the serving stack,
precision and quantization; measure it. It is a significant advantage over
bottleneck adapters [@houlsby2019parameter], which insert extra layers.

Or you can *not* merge, keep the base shared in memory, and swap adapters per
request:

| tenants | one shared base + adapters | a separate 8B copy each | ratio |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 10 | 15.7 GiB | 149.6 GiB | 9.5× |
| 100 | 22.8 GiB | 1,495.7 GiB | 65.7× |
| 1,000 | 93.1 GiB | 14,957.0 GiB | 160.7× |

The adapter size those rows assume is an $r{=}16$ adapter on attention *and*
MLP, saved in bf16: $41{,}943{,}040 \times 2$ bytes, exactly 80 MiB. Change
either choice and the figure moves a long way — `q_proj, v_proj` only at the
same rank is 6.82M parameters, 13 MiB, and `peft` will happily save the same
adapter in fp32 and double whatever you expected. [Always state targets and
dtype when you quote an adapter size]{.hl}; on its own the rank tells you
almost nothing.

Even at the generous end, the weights of a thousand customers' private
fine-tunes — one bf16 base and a thousand adapters — come to 93.1 GiB. That is
a *weight-storage* sum; it does not show that one node can serve a thousand
tenants at the concurrency and latency you need: KV caches, adapter loading,
workspace and traffic have to be budgeted separately. Still, it is one reason
"fine-tuning" can be a product at all, rather than a research technique —
and it is worth noticing that the paper made the same point about GPT-3 in
2021: 100 adapted models cost 350 GB + 35 MB × 100 ≈ 354 GB, against 35 TB for
100 separate copies [@hu2022lora].

## Preference and reward optimization {#sec-preference}

### The thing supervised fine-tuning cannot do

Take a question with no single right answer:

```text
Kredi kartı borcumu nasıl kapatabilirim?
(How can I pay off my credit card debt?)
```

There is no single required answer. There are a thousand acceptable answers
and they differ along axes you can *recognise* but find hard to *write down* as
rules: too curt, too long, too confident about your finances, gives advice it
should have refused to give, correct but reads like a pamphlet. A chosen, safe
and helpful answer can still be written as an SFT target. The real distinction
is the kind of supervision you have: if you can write acceptable example
answers, SFT fits; if you can judge the relative quality of two candidates more
reliably, preference pairs add a signal.

But you can still do something: show two candidate answers to a person and ask
which is better. The result is a
[preference pair](#gloss-preference-pair){#term-preference-pair .term-ref}. For
some tasks producing one is an easier judgement than writing the ideal answer,
and one you can collect from people who could not have written either answer
themselves; but labellers need clear criteria, expertise where the task needs
it, and a check on disagreement.

::: {#gloss-preference-pair .column-margin .term-gloss}
**preference pair** — one prompt, two candidate answers, and a label saying
which was preferred. On its own a binary preference does not measure either
answer's absolute adequacy; both may be poor.
[↩](#term-preference-pair){.term-back}
:::

[Preference optimization turns the relative order of two candidates directly
into a training signal]{.hl} [@christiano2017deep]. The chosen answers can be
used for SFT too; the difference is how the comparison, and the rejected
answer's information, enter the loss.

### RLHF: the four-model dance

The original recipe,
reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
[@stiennon2020learning; @ouyang2022training], turns those
comparisons into a training signal in two steps: fit a
[reward model](#gloss-reward-model){#term-reward-model .term-ref} to the
preferences, then optimize the language model against it.


Two words from reinforcement learning appear from here on. The **policy** is
simply the model being trained, seen as defining a probability distribution
over possible answers (token by token) given a prompt. The **KL divergence**
$\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}[\pi \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}]$ measures how far one
probability distribution has moved from another; it is zero when the two are
identical and grows as they separate. Here it compares the policy's answer
distribution with the frozen reference's, averaged over prompts in the
training objective.

::: {#gloss-reward-model .column-margin .term-gloss}
**reward model** — a model trained on human comparisons that reads a prompt and
an answer and returns one number. It exists to turn *A is better than B* into
something an optimizer can maximise.
[↩](#term-reward-model){.term-back}
:::

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}

     aria-label="A two-phase diagram. Phase one, on the left, shows a prompt producing two candidate answers, a human choosing the better one, and that comparison training a reward model that outputs a single scalar score. Phase two, on the right, shows a training loop with four components: the policy being trained, a frozen reference copy of it used to compute a KL penalty, the frozen reward model that scores samples, and a value model that estimates expected return. The reward model is the interesting object: it converts an *ordering* — A beat
B — into a *scalar*, which is what a reinforcement-learning algorithm needs.
The diagram shows the four functions of InstructGPT-style PPO-based RLHF: the
policy being updated, a frozen reference, the reward model and a value
component for advantage estimation. They need not be separate networks, nor
held on one GPU at once (the value estimator can share the trunk, components
can sit on different devices); the memory cost depends on the implementation.
The reinforcement-learning algorithm in the middle is PPO [@schulman2017ppo],
one of the methods used to update the policy.
:::
::::

The result was not marginal. On the prompts studied, human labellers
preferred the outputs of InstructGPT's 1.3B model, put through this pipeline,
to those of the 175B GPT-3 — "despite having 100x fewer parameters"
[@ouyang2022training]. That is a preference for particular answers, not a
general capability advantage. The cost figure is separate and belongs to the
study's 175B version: training the 175B SFT model took 4.9 petaflop/s-days and the 175B
PPO-ptx model 60, "compared to 3,640 petaflops/s-days for GPT-3"
[@ouyang2022training]. [The reported SFT and PPO-ptx runs together cost about 1.8% of what pretraining cost, and that total leaves out the reward model.]{.hl}

::: {.column-margin}
That comparison is the strongest single argument in this chapter for taking
post-training seriously. It is also a good argument against believing that
parameter count alone tells you what a model can do.
:::

### DPO: deriving the shortcut away

Look again at the diagram and ask which box is doing indispensable work. The
reward model exists only to score samples during PPO. If the policy's
probabilities, read as a log-ratio against the reference, could serve as a
reward, the box would not need training separately.

In the KL-regularized preference objective, they can. This is the
[direct preference optimization](#gloss-direct-preference-optimization){#term-direct-preference-optimization .term-ref}
result [@rafailov2023dpo]: it re-expresses the reward through the log-ratio of
policy and reference, so training on preference pairs needs no separate reward
network and no PPO sampling loop. The preference data and the reward-modelling
assumption do not go away, and the derivation is worth stating because it is
short and the conclusion is otherwise mystifying.

::: {#gloss-direct-preference-optimization .column-margin .term-gloss}
**direct preference optimization** — training the policy on preference pairs
with a loss derived from reparameterising the KL-regularized reward objective.
It needs no separate reward network and no sampling during training; how well
it works depends on its assumptions and on how well the data fit. Usually
written *DPO*.
[↩](#term-direct-preference-optimization){.term-back}
:::

Before the shortcut, the two objectives it is a shortcut *around*, because the
derivation below leans on both. First, the reward model is fitted to the
comparisons with the **Bradley–Terry** likelihood — the assumption that a person
prefers $y_w$ over $y_l$ with probability $\sigma(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l))$. Here
$y_w$ is the preferred (*winning*) answer, $y_l$ the rejected (*losing*) one,
and $\sigma$ the logistic function. If you know chess ratings, this is the same
model as Elo: only the difference between two scores decides who is expected
to win.

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{RM}} = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(x, y_w, y_l)}\left[\log \sigma\!\left(r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l)\right)\right]
$$

Only *differences* of $r_\phi$ within a prompt are constrained, so rewards are
identified only up to an additive function of $x$: add the same $f(x)$ to every
response and nothing changes. Do not read that as "the scale is arbitrary".
Doubling every reward does change the model — $\sigma(1) = 0.731$ against
$\sigma(2) = 0.881$ — unless you rescale the link temperature to match. The
additive freedom is what makes the $Z(x)$ term cancel a few lines from now,
because the offset is the same for both responses to one prompt.

Second, the policy is optimised against that frozen reward, leashed to the
reference:

$$
\max_{\pi_\theta}\; \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathcal{D}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)}\big[r_\phi(x, y)\big]
\;-\; \beta\, \mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}\!\left[\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid x)\right]\Big]
$$

The number $\beta$ is the strength of the leash. A large $\beta$ keeps the
policy close to the reference and gives up some reward; a small $\beta$ lets it
chase the reward further — and, with a learned reward model, closer to reward
hacking.

PPO is one way of taking a step on that objective: it maximises a clipped
surrogate so that a single batch cannot move the policy far
[@schulman2017ppo]. That clip range is one of the hyperparameters the table
below charges to PPO's account.

*That* objective — maximise reward, penalised by KL divergence from the
reference — has a known closed-form optimum:

$$
\pi^{*}(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)} \, \pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x) \, \exp\!\left( \frac{1}{\beta} r(x, y) \right)
$$

Rearrange for $r$:

$$
r(x, y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi^{*}(y \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y \mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x)
$$

[In this derivation the reward is represented, up to a term that depends only
on the prompt, as the log-ratio of policy and reference.]{.hl} That does not
make learned reward models pointless; it means that, under these assumptions,
the policy can be updated on preference pairs without training a separate
reward model. And the awkward $Z(x)$ — a sum over every possible response, which is why nobody computes it —
depends only on the prompt, so it cancels the moment you compare two responses
to the *same* prompt. Which is precisely what preference data gives you.

Substituting into the Bradley–Terry model of pairwise preference leaves an
ordinary supervised loss over preference pairs $(x, y_w, y_l)$:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\,\mathbb{E}\left[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w \mid x)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l \mid x)} \right) \right]
$$

Read it in words and it stops being intimidating: *make the preferred answer's
log-probability ratio against the reference larger than the rejected answer's,
so you are rewarded for moving in the right direction rather than for agreeing
with the reference.* The loss does not fix the direction of either probability
on its own.

One precision on "raise" and "lower". The loss only asks for the *gap* between
the two log-ratios to widen. In practice both probabilities often fall during
DPO, the rejected one faster, so do not be surprised if the preferred answer's
own likelihood goes down while the loss improves.

Notice what $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is doing here, because it is the reason for the
*"avoid DPO on a base model"* advice you will meet later.

DPO's setup assumes the preference pairs were sampled from the reference. So the
paper sets $\pi_{\text{ref}} = \pi_{\text{SFT}}$ whenever an SFT model
exists — and when one does not, it recommends fine-tuning on the *preferred*
completions first and using that, explicitly "to mitigate the distribution
shift between the true reference distribution which is unavailable, and
$\pi_{\text{ref}}$ used by DPO" [@rafailov2023dpo].

Which locates one likely failure. [The loss never samples anything; if the
preference pairs come from an instruction-following model, a base model is a
weak reference, and the problem is the mismatch between reference and data, not
an inability to "rank".]{.hl} DPO on a base model is mathematically well
defined; whether it works depends on data coverage, the choice of reference and
the task evaluation.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**What the substitution actually bought.**

| | PPO-based RLHF | offline DPO |
|:--|:--|:--|
| components | policy, reference, reward and value functions | policy + reference probabilities (can be precomputed) |
| separate reward model | usually trained first | not needed |
| sampling during training | yes, the policy generates | no, existing pairs are used (online variants do generate) |
| what a step is | a reinforcement-learning update | a gradient step on a classification loss |
| tuning burden | PPO's clip range, value loss, GAE, plus $\beta$ | $\beta$, plus the learning rate |

DPO removes the two things practitioners often complained about — the separate
reward model and the generation loop — which reduces setup and compute cost for
many teams.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**What DPO did not remove.** You still need reliable preference labels and an
evaluation of their coverage; labelling can be done by people, by a model or by
a verifier, and its cost depends on the method. DPO makes the *algorithm*
cheap, not the *data*. It also inherits a subtler problem: if the pairs were
collected once, from some other model's outputs, they can represent your policy
less well as it moves away from whatever generated them. In the Tülu 3 study,
on-policy preference data — generated by the model being trained — improved
downstream results over reused off-policy pairs [@lambert2025tulu3]; do not
assume the same gain for every corpus.
:::

### GRPO: delete the value model instead

DPO deletes the reward model. GRPO [@shao2024deepseekmath] takes the other
route: keep reinforcement learning, but delete the *value* model.

The value model exists to supply a baseline. In policy-gradient methods you do
not want the raw reward — you want to know whether an action was better
**than expected**, because a reward of 8 means something different when your
usual score is 2 than when it is 9. Training an estimator of that expectation
is the standard answer, and it costs something: a separate model or a head
sharing the policy's trunk, with a memory cost that depends on the training
setup.

GRPO's observation is that if you are going to sample from the policy anyway,
you can get a baseline without training a separate value estimator — though
generating and scoring several answers per prompt has its own compute cost. Sample $G$ answers **to the same prompt**,
score them all, and use the group's own mean as the expectation:

$$
A_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}{\operatorname{std}(r_1, \ldots, r_G)}
$$

$A_i$ is called the **advantage** of answer $i$: positive means "better than
this group's average", and the update makes that answer more likely; negative
makes it less likely. Dividing by the standard deviation puts every prompt on
the same scale, so easy and hard prompts pull with comparable force. One
consequence to remember: if all $G$ answers get the same reward — all right or
all wrong — every $A_i$ is zero (implementations add a tiny constant to avoid
dividing by zero, or skip the group), and that prompt gives no signal from the
reward comparison; other terms such as the KL can still act.

The question stops being *how good is this answer in absolute terms* and
becomes *was this attempt better than my other attempts at the same question*
— a relative signal that needs no separate value model. How stable it is
depends on $G$, the reward distribution and the normalisation; a small $G$ can
bring high variance. GRPO still keeps the
frozen reference and the KL leash, and it still needs *some* reward — a reward
model or, as the next section shows, a checker. In the paper's words (*critic*
is another name for the value model),
GRPO "foregoes the critic model, instead estimating the baseline from group
scores, significantly reducing training resources" [@shao2024deepseekmath].
On DeepSeekMath-Instruct 7B it moved GSM8K from 82.9% to 88.2% and MATH from
46.8% to 51.7%, using only instruction-tuning data already in hand — a result
of that setup, not something to credit to the group mean alone.

### Where the reward comes from, and why that is the real question

There is one more move, and it is among the ones that have shaped the field
most recently. Most of the methods above assumed the reward is *learned* — from human
comparisons, so it inherits every flaw of a learned model, including being
gameable.

For some tasks it does not have to be. If the answer is a number, check the
number. If it is code, run the tests. DeepSeek-R1-Zero — the variant trained by
reinforcement learning with no supervised warm-up — uses "rule-based rewards"
of two kinds: **accuracy rewards**, which evaluate whether the final answer is
correct on tasks such as maths and code (the answer is asked for in a specified
format so it can be checked), and **format rewards**, which check that the
reasoning was placed where it was asked to be [@guo2025deepseekr1]. Tülu 3
builds the same idea into an open recipe under the name **RLVR**, reinforcement
learning with verifiable rewards [@lambert2025tulu3].

::: {.column-margin}
This is also the sharpest limitation. Verifiable rewards need a verifier, and
most things people want from a language model — was this summary faithful, was
this tone appropriate, was this refusal correct — have no verifier. Maths and
code are unusually lucky domains. @sec-reasoning follows what happens
when you push this idea as far as it goes.
:::

The trade, roughly: a learned reward model can approximately judge open-ended
qualities but is limited by the coverage of its labels and can be gamed; a
rule-based verifier gives a strong signal on the narrow set of tasks whose
correctness a criterion can check, and is usually harder to game — but only as
far as its specification and implementation go. A test suite with gaps rewards
a program that hard-codes the visible cases; a loose answer parser rewards
whatever matches its regex (@sec-reasoning has the version of this that bites
in practice). Because the two kinds of reward fail in different ways, many
recipes use both, on different subsets of the data; which to use is decided by
the verifiable part of the task and the behaviour you want.

### Choosing, by what data you have

Strip the acronyms and every method above is a claim about what you can
collect.

| you have | worth trying | what it costs you, what else it needs |
|:--|:--|:--|
| prompts with ideal answers written out | **SFT** | writing the answers; a task evaluation |
| pairs of answers with a "which is better" label (from people, a model or a verifier) | **DPO** | annotation; a matching reference and label coverage |
| a preference/reward signal and a budget for online RL | **RLHF/PPO** | a generation loop, reward and value computation; hard to tune |
| prompts whose answers can be scored | **GRPO** (often with verifiable rewards) | a reward function, and a lot of sampling |
| a stronger model whose outputs you may use | **distillation** (@sec-distillation) | inference bills, licence and quality measurement |

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**The order to try things in, for a team of one or two.** First set up a
baseline with prompting, an output schema and, if needed, retrieval
(@sec-decision-tree). If you have examples of the behaviour, try SFT. Compare
DPO when you have a *specific* complaint about the SFT model's behaviour that
you can express as pairs — "it should have refused this", "it should have been
shorter". Consider an RL loop only if it buys a measurable gain on the target
task in exchange for the extra generation and reward-evaluation compute; the
reward can come from a verifier or a vetted reward model, but with the latter
you sign up to maintain a reward model as well as a policy.
:::

## Constitutional AI and feedback that isn't human {#sec-rlaif}

Where rule-based rewards do not apply, the bottleneck is often annotation.
Constitutional AI [@bai2022constitutional] studies how a model can produce
harmlessness feedback with less dependence on human labels.

The method has two halves. In the supervised half, the model answers a
red-team prompt, then **critiques its own answer** against a written
principle, then **revises** it; the revision becomes the training target. In
the RL half, the same principles are used to label preference pairs for
harmlessness, replacing the human annotator there — reinforcement learning
from AI feedback, RLAIF. (In the paper, the helpfulness comparisons were still
labelled by people.)

::: {.column-margin}
Anthropic's team wrote 16 principles for the harmlessness experiments and
sampled one at random at each critique-and-revision step
[@bai2022constitutional]. The randomisation was not for fairness: they found
that ensembling over principles produced notably more robust preference-model
behaviour than using one principle for every label.
:::

Two things about this are worth separating, because they are usually praised
together and only one of them is unambiguous.

**What is clearly good:** the principles are an *artefact*. They are a text
file. You can read them, argue with them, version them, and hand them to a
regulator. Human preference data can also have guidelines and quality control
behind it, but when those are unpublished the values can only be recovered by
probing the finished model. Moving the specification into a document helps
accountability, independent of whether the technique works better; a written
principle still does not prove on its own that behaviour follows it.

**What is not settled:** AI feedback can carry the evaluator model's errors and
biases into the training signal. The evaluator is often the same model as the
one being trained, or a close relative, and then shared blind spots need
particular scrutiny. Where it cannot tell that an answer is subtly wrong, the
training signal is confidently wrong, and scale alone does not fix a bias
shared by both sides of the loop. A reasonable expectation is that AI feedback
is more reliable on properties a model can check (is this rude, does this
contain the requested section, does this refuse) and less reliable where
checking needs domain expertise; but measure that per criterion against
human- and expert-checked examples.

## Distillation into something you can afford {#sec-distillation}

Everything so far has made a model *better*.
[Knowledge distillation](#gloss-knowledge-distillation){#term-knowledge-distillation .term-ref}
[@hinton2015distilling] aims to transfer a large teacher's behaviour to a
smaller student, which can be *cheaper* to serve. Measure the overall gain
together with the cost of generating the teacher data and training the
student.

::: {#gloss-knowledge-distillation .column-margin .term-gloss}
**knowledge distillation** — training a small student on a teacher's
probability distribution or on selected outputs. What the student learns
depends on the data, its capacity and the evaluation; inheriting the teacher's
mistakes is a risk, which filtering the outputs can reduce.
[↩](#term-knowledge-distillation){.term-back}
:::

The setup: a large **teacher** produces outputs, a small **student** is trained
to reproduce them. In the classical form the student matches the teacher's
full output distribution — its "soft targets" — which can carry more
information per example than a hard label does. Knowing that the teacher put
70% on *positive*, 25% on *neutral*, and 5% on *negative* tells the student
that this example is borderline; a one-hot label of *positive* does not. How
useful that is depends on the teacher's calibration and the task.

For generative models the modern form is blunter and works well: have the
teacher answer a large set of prompts, filter the answers, and fine-tune the
student on them as ordinary SFT data. DeepSeek-R1's authors did exactly this,
using 800,000 curated samples from their large model to train small dense
models [@guo2025deepseekr1].

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**When does a small distilled student pay?** Usually not on capability but on
cost per correct answer. On a narrow, frequently repeated task, if the student
clears your quality bar and the traffic covers the cost of teacher data and
training, it can lower total cost: a large model may need a long instruction
prefix, while the student has the instruction baked into its weights. When you
compute cost per correct answer, count prompt and output tokens, caching,
retries, the verifier's cost and the cost of errors; a 1B-versus-70B comparison
says nothing general until it is measured on the target task.

The condition is narrowness. Distil a general assistant into 1B parameters and
you get a worse general assistant.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Check the terms before you use a teacher's outputs.** Hosted services' terms
of use and open-weight models' licences can set different conditions on using
outputs to train another model: some restrict it, some permit it, some require
attribution in the derived model's name (the Llama 3.1 licence is one,
@sec-model-cards). This is a contract question, not a technical one: read the
terms of the specific version of the model, service and dataset you will use,
and get your organisation's legal review if needed.
:::

## Continued pretraining, and the Turkish case {#sec-continued-pretraining}

There is a situation where the "post-training is not a reliable way to add
knowledge" principle bends: when what is missing is not a fact but a
*distribution*. A model that has seen little Turkish is not missing one fact
about Turkish; it is missing the patterns of the language. But if a model does
poorly in Turkish, first measure why on the target tasks: the data mix, the
tokenizer, model size and instruction tuning each have their own effect.

The tool for that is **continued pretraining**: take the base model and keep
running stage 1 on a domain corpus, with the same next-token objective and no
instruction format at all [@gururangan2020dont]. It sits between the stages —
pretraining's objective, with a data and compute need that depends on the
corpus and the goal rather than being fixed in advance.

::: {#gloss-continued-pretraining .column-margin .term-gloss}
**continued pretraining** — running the pretraining objective again on a
narrower corpus, starting from an existing base model. Used when the gap is a
whole domain or language rather than a task or a format.
[↩](#term-continued-pretraining){.term-back}
:::

For Turkish you have three options, and @sec-tokenizer-budget already measured
the token side of one of them for you:

| route | possible benefit | risk and cost to measure |
|:--|:--|:--|
| adapt a multilingual model to the task | fastest path; builds on the ready model's existing abilities | Turkish task quality; Turkish token counts under that model's tokenizer; adaptation compute |
| [continued pretraining](#gloss-continued-pretraining){#term-continued-pretraining .term-ref} on a Turkish corpus, then task adaptation | may strengthen language and domain patterns | corpus and training cost (a real, if small, pretraining run); regression in general abilities |
| start from a Turkish-native model | fewer tokens on target text (lower fertility) and possibly better-suited representations | task quality, licence, size and serving cost; available Turkish-native models are mostly small |

The token side is measurable, and we measured it in @sec-pretraining: on the
same Turkish text Llama 3's tokenizer produces **2.12** tokens per word against
**1.59** for BERTurk's; a *token-count difference* of about **33%**. They belong
to different models; you cannot put BERTurk's tokenizer on Llama 3. So the
difference is not an automatic 33% bill or latency increase for one model but a
token gap between two candidates; decide with each candidate's own tokenizer,
task quality and real price. (This is a different comparison from the 23% in
@sec-tokenizer-budget: there we compared the same content in Turkish and
English, here the same Turkish text under two tokenizers.) For a concrete map of
Turkish-first models and for deciding between multilingual and monolingual
with a measurement, see @sec-turkish-nlp-ecosystem and
@sec-turkish-nlp-decide.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Compare by task.** For classification or extraction on short texts, compare
Turkish-first and multilingual candidates on the same held-out data for
quality, latency and cost; @sec-lora-lab shows a 110M-parameter Turkish-first
model doing well on one task, but only that task. If the task needs broad
knowledge or reasoning, add tests for it; the Turkish-first models you can
afford may lag multilingual ones there. Consider continued pretraining with a
pilot run if you have enough Turkish text and a measured quality gap, and
measure regression in existing abilities too.
:::

## When not to fine-tune {#sec-decision-tree}

Most of this chapter has been about how. This section is about *whether*, and
it is the part to remember if you remember one part.

There is a common failure mode. A team has a model that gets things wrong about
their business. Fine-tuning is the technique that sounds like "teach the model
about our business". They collect examples, run a LoRA job, and the model can
come back **more fluent and still wrong** — because the examples taught it the
*style* of their documentation without giving it the current *contents* in a
form it can reliably recall. First test where the wrong information comes from
and how the right source can be put in front of the model.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Which technique, and why — walk it top to bottom</div>

     aria-label="A decision tree with five questions asked in order. Question one: is the missing thing a fact the model could not have known, such as your documents, your prices, or this week's events? If yes, use retrieval, because fine-tuning on facts produces a model that is fluent and still wrong. Question two: have you actually tried a better prompt, few-shot examples, or a constrained output schema on twenty real inputs? If no, do that first, because its starting cost is low and it is often enough. Question three: do you have at least a few hundred examples of the behaviour you want, or can you write them? If no, collect the data, which is the honest answer most of the time. Question four: is the complaint about what the model says, or about which of two acceptable answers is better? If it is what it says, use supervised fine-tuning with LoRA. If it is which is better, use DPO on preference pairs with a matching reference; an SFT start is often helpful.
