The tree starts from the options with low setup cost and separates kinds of
problem, and every exit before question 4 is a way of *not* running a training
job; the branches are not a universal price ranking. A fine-tune needs
maintenance together with its training data and a regression evaluation: when
the base model updates it has to be re-evaluated and often retrained. Prompts,
retrieval and schemas also need re-testing when the model version changes, but
that upkeep is usually lighter.
:::
::::

::: {.column-margin}
Branch 2 is not a formality. "Have you tried a better prompt" is a question
with a large literature behind it — one survey catalogues 58 distinct
text-only prompting techniques [@schulhoff2025prompt], and @sec-prompting works
through the ones that matter. Teams who reach for fine-tuning have often tried
only a few.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The two rules the tree encodes.**

1. **Retrieval first for knowledge, fine-tuning if needed for behaviour.** If
   the error comes from missing current or organisation-specific information,
   first supply and verify the source through retrieval; for behaviour, try
   prompting and, if needed, fine-tuning. They are not alternatives; they can
   compose: a common and strong architecture is a model that has learned your
   *format and tone*, answering over retrieved documents that supply your
   *facts*. This is a starting intuition, not a strict split: knowledge can also
   be added by continued pretraining, and behaviour can change with a
   prompt.
2. **Do not DPO straight from a base model.** DPO's loss compares the policy
   against a frozen reference on two *fixed* completions, and it works best when
   those completions look like things the reference would produce. A base model
   is a poor reference for preference data written by an instruction-following
   model, and the objective spends itself on that mismatch instead of on the
   preference. Nothing in the loss forbids it — this is a statement about
   distribution match, not a definedness condition — but SFT first is the
   recipe that works.
:::

## Catastrophic forgetting {#sec-forgetting}

There is one more cost, and it does not appear on any invoice.

A fine-tune moves weights, and weights carry shared representations: the
parameters that help represent *how to classify a Turkish review* can also
contribute to representing *Turkish*. A model can improve on the new task while
regressing on tasks it used to do well — the phenomenon called
[catastrophic forgetting](#gloss-catastrophic-forgetting){#term-catastrophic-forgetting .term-ref}
[@kirkpatrick2017overcoming]. It has also been observed in large language
models during continual fine-tuning [@luo2025empirical]; its size depends on
the training and the evaluation.

::: {#gloss-catastrophic-forgetting .column-margin .term-gloss}
**catastrophic forgetting** — when training on a new task degrades performance
on tasks the model previously handled, because the two relied on shared
representations. It is invisible unless you evaluate the old task on
purpose.
[↩](#term-catastrophic-forgetting){.term-back}
:::

The reason it is dangerous is not that it happens. It is that **your evaluation
will not show it**. You built a test set for your task. Your fine-tune improves
on your test set. Every number you look at goes up. If something went down,
it is something you were not measuring, and you may find out from a user.
Choose the abilities you want to keep before adapting, and measure them on the
same held-out examples before and after.

### Measuring it on our own model

We can do better than assert this. Take the same BERTurk model and the same
Turkish reviews task from @sec-bake-off, fine-tune it two ways, and then ask a
question that has nothing to do with sentiment: *how well does the encoder
still model Turkish?*

The probe is the original pretraining objective. Mask 15% of the tokens in
held-out Turkish text and measure the mean cross-entropy of the model's own
masked-language head at those positions, before and after. This is a
*masked-language-modelling probe*; it is not directly comparable with the
autoregressive perplexity in @sec-language-models.

One methodological point decides whether the numbers mean anything. In the
LoRA row the adapter is *active*: here it was probed **merged into the base
weights**. (Merging is not required; in the re-run the merged model and the
model with the adapter active differed by at most $4.8\times10^{-6}$ in any
logit, in fp32.) Deleting the adapter would recover the starting model and the
measurement would be a tautology. What is being asked is: *when you deploy the
LoRA-adapted model, has that model's grip on Turkish loosened?*

One limit of the probe, stated before the numbers rather than after. The
masked-language head is frozen at its pretrained weights while the encoder
underneath moves, so a rising loss measures *the encoder drifting away from
that head* — which mixes genuine loss of linguistic information with a
representation the old head can no longer read. Those are not the same thing,
and this design cannot separate them. What would separate them is a freshly
fitted probe on top of each encoder, or a downstream Turkish task the encoder
has not been tuned on. Read the table as a change in fit seen through the
existing frozen head, not as a measurement of how much Turkish knowledge was
lost.

Two probe sets, because they answer different questions. **General Turkish** is
1,826 sentences of ordinary prose from a parallel corpus [@zhang2020improving] —
nothing to do with reviews, nothing to do with sentiment. **Held-out reviews**
is the test split from the lab below (@sec-lora-lab): same domain as the fine-tune, included so
that nobody can dismiss the result as a domain-shift artefact. The masked
tensors are generated once and reused for all three encoders, which removes
sampling differences; the evaluation mode, the MLM head and the numerical
precision should be held equal too.

| encoder | general TR loss | top-1 | reviews loss | top-1 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| pretrained, untouched | 2.523 | 50.7% | 2.660 | 48.3% |
| after a full fine-tune | 2.837 *(+12.5%)* | 46.4% | 4.564 *(+71.6%)* | 28.9% |
| after LoRA $r=8$, merged | 2.592 *(+2.7%)* | 49.6% | 3.276 *(+23.2%)* | 42.0% |

::: {.column-margin}
Loss is mean cross-entropy in nats over masked positions — 5,406 of them for
general Turkish, 9,893 for the reviews — and top-1 is how often the model's
single best guess is the token that was actually there. Lower loss and higher
top-1 are both better, and the base row is the model as the Hub ships it.
:::

The probe's code had not been saved; we rewrote it from the text and ran it
(re-run, October 2026). For general Turkish we used the Turkish side of the
OPUS-100 `en-tr` test split (1,976 deduplicated sentences, 2,860 masked
positions), for reviews the first 2,000 reviews of the test split (9,753
positions); the full fine-tune is our 2e-5 run (85.34 macro-F1), and LoRA
$r=8$ is the run that reproduces the book's lab row exactly. The pretrained
model scored 2.897 loss and 47.0% top-1 on general Turkish, 2.602 and 49.1% on
reviews. After the full fine-tune the loss rose **+9.7%** on general Turkish
(top-1 44.1%) and **+55.5%** on reviews (35.0%); with merged LoRA the rises were
**+1.7%** (46.2%) and **+25.9%** (42.2%). Because the text and the full
fine-tune's settings differ, the magnitudes differ from the book's table; the
ordering and the in-domain pattern are the same.

Three things in that table are worth more than the paragraph that introduced
them.

**Both adaptations look worse under the old head, and the full one by about
4.6× more.** Say what that ratio is: 12.5% against 2.7% is a ratio of *relative
loss increases* measured through a frozen head, not a measurement that one model
forgot 4.6 times as much Turkish. On text that has nothing to do with the task,
a full fine-tune raises the masked-language loss measured through the frozen
head by 12.5% and costs four points of top-1 accuracy. That is not catastrophic
in the dramatic sense, but it is a meaningful regression under this probe; it
does not show that the model's general Turkish ability fell by the same share.
Test the product abilities you want to keep separately.

**In this experiment LoRA's loss increase is smaller than the full fine-tune's,
but not zero.** +2.7% is small, but it is not zero, and the merged model reads measurably worse through the head it started
with. Anyone who tells you parameter-efficient tuning cannot forget is quoting
the reversibility argument and calling it the forgetting argument.

**The regression is larger on the in-domain probe.** This is the row that
surprises people: the full fine-tune's loss rises 12.5% on general Turkish and
**71.6%** on held-out reviews — nearly six times as much on the domain it was
trained on (9.7% against 55.5% in the re-run). One possible reading: the model
reorganises, for the task, the representations your data touched most — review
text shifts from *"everything a sentence can mean"* towards *"which of two
buttons to press"* — and the masked-language head can no longer read it as
well. How much of that is representational change and how much a mismatch with
the old head, this design cannot separate. The practical point stands: in this
experiment the probe most sensitive to regression was the in-domain one, which
is exactly the kind of probe that looks redundant next to the task test set and
so does not get built.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Both probes deteriorated while the number you were watching improved.**
Loss rose and top-1 fell on every row and every probe set; the sentiment score
went the other way. The full fine-tune is the best sentiment model in the lab — 83.90
macro-F1, the top of that table — and it is the weakest of the three under this
probe, on both sets. Neither fact is visible from the other's evaluation. This is the
trap in its exact shape: not a model that got worse, but a model that got
better at the one thing you measured.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Two different advantages, often confused.** Keep them apart.

The first is **reversibility**, and it is arithmetic rather than empirical.
With LoRA the base weights are never written to; the adapter is a separate pair
of matrices. Remove the adapter with the same base checkpoint, dtype and
loading setup and the starting outputs come back. A full fine-tune can be
undone too if you kept the base checkpoint; the difference is that the task
update is not managed as a separate, small file. That is why you should record
the exact revision hash of the base you used.

The second is **reduced forgetting in the merged model**, and it is not
guaranteed by the first. $W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ is a genuinely different
matrix from $W_0$; nothing stops it from being a *worse* Turkish model. What
constrains it is that the update is confined to a rank-$r$ subspace of two
projections per layer, so there is far less room to move than a full fine-tune
has. That is a plausible mechanism, not a proof — which is exactly why the row
above is measured rather than asserted.
:::

### What to do about it

The field's standard answer is the one InstructGPT used. Having found
"performance regressions on public NLP datasets" — the **alignment tax** —
the authors mixed pretraining gradients back into the RLHF update, producing
the variant they call PPO-ptx, and reported that this minimises the
regressions [@ouyang2022training]. The principle generalises: *if you do not
want the model to forget something, keep showing it to the model.*

In practice, three habits catch almost everything:

| habit | what it costs | what it catches |
|:--|:--|:--|
| pick a general benchmark **before** training and run it both times | one evaluation run | the existence of the problem |
| mix 5–10% general data into your fine-tuning set | slightly slower convergence | most of the damage |
| prefer LoRA at a modest rank over a full fine-tune | about a point of macro-F1, in our lab | roughly four fifths of the damage, measured above — plus an undo |

::: {.column-margin}
"Before training" is doing real work in row one. A benchmark chosen after you
see the fine-tuned model's failures is a benchmark chosen to make the model
look good on the failures you happened to notice.
:::

## Lab: LoRA on a Turkish task, measured {#sec-lora-lab}

This section looks at the same Turkish product-review task from @sec-bake-off,
run seven ways on one Apple M-series GPU, with the numbers reported as they
came out. They are observations of this setup; do not carry them directly to
other hardware or another split.

The setup is deliberately modest, because the point is that this is reachable.
BERTurk base (`dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased`, 110.6M parameters), the
@sec-bake-off split — 40,000 training reviews, 10,000 held out, seed 42 — two
epochs, sequence length 128, batch size 32, on an Apple M-series GPU. LoRA
adapters on `query` and `value` only, $\alpha = 2r$, dropout 0.05. The original
runs' code, software versions and learning rate were not recorded; the re-run
below says how we filled the gaps.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The limit of the comparison.** All rows were run at one shared learning rate,
so the gap between full fine-tuning and LoRA does not show each method's
separately tuned best. The rank rows are comparable at the shared rate, though
each rank's best rate may differ too. For a reliable method comparison, search
each method's rate on a validation slice held out of the training split; do not
use the test set for the choice. The re-run measured how much this limit
matters (below).
:::

| what we trained | trainable | share | macro-F1 | F1(neg) | accuracy | wall clock | peak GiB |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| head only (a linear probe) | 1,538 | 0.001% | 48.37 | 0.00 | 93.68 | 3m 35s | 0.41 |
| full fine-tune | 110,618,882 | 100% | **83.90** | **70.16** | 95.62 | 11m 59s | 6.07 |
| LoRA $r=1$ | 38,402 | 0.035% | 80.47 | 63.01 | 96.09 | 10m 01s | 4.32 |
| LoRA $r=4$ | 148,994 | 0.135% | 80.50 | 62.97 | 96.26 | 9m 46s | 4.32 |
| LoRA $r=8$ | 296,450 | 0.267% | 82.69 | 67.23 | 96.50 | 10m 04s | 4.32 |
| LoRA $r=16$ | 591,362 | 0.532% | 82.59 | 66.99 | **96.58** | 10m 03s | 4.33 |
| LoRA $r=64$ | 2,360,834 | 2.090% | 82.39 | 66.60 | 96.55 | 10m 30s | 4.37 |

For reference, @sec-bake-off's best non-neural model on this same split — tf-idf
over word 1-2 grams, no GPU — scored **76.21** macro-F1 and **56.47** F1(neg).

::: {.column-margin}
"Peak GiB" is the largest live MPS allocation measured in this study, in a
fresh process per row. It is not the operating system's total GPU or shared
memory use: the MPS driver's own high-water mark runs about 0.7 GiB higher
across the rows. The re-run showed that *when* the column is sampled matters
too (below). For real device planning, use the same measurement method and
batch/sequence conditions.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Re-run (October 2026).** The lab's code had not been saved; we rewrote it from
the text and ran it on the same split (exactly the same 40,000/10,000, test
93.68% positive) on an Apple M5 Max. Details the text does not give are our
choice: AdamW, weight decay 0, linearly decaying rate, no warm-up.

*The shared rate.* We ran LoRA $r=8$ at several rates; at 2e-4 it gave
**82.66 / 67.17 / 96.51%** against the table's 82.69 / 67.23 / 96.50% — very
likely the table's shared rate. At the same 2e-4, full fine-tuning *diverged*
in our setup and collapsed to the majority class (10% warm-up or gradient
clipping at 1.0 did not rescue it), so the table's full-fine-tune row cannot be
reproduced in this setup. How decisive the shared rate is, is plain: LoRA
$r=8$ collapsed to the majority class at 2e-5 (48.37), scored 75.57 at 5e-5 and
81.50 at 1e-4; full fine-tuning scored 85.70 at 2e-5, 85.23 at 5e-5 and 84.20 at
1e-4.

*Per-method tuning.* On a 4,000-review validation slice held out of the
training set, the best rate was 2e-5 for full fine-tuning (83.69) and 1e-3 for
LoRA $r=8$ (82.64; 2e-3 diverged) — about fifty times higher. At those rates the
test scores were **85.37 ± 0.47** for full fine-tuning (four runs) and
**83.68 ± 0.40** for LoRA $r=8$ (three seeds). Tuning shrinks the gap from 2.7
points at the shared rate to 1.7, but does not close it; the remaining gap is
larger than the seed noise.

*Other rows (2e-4, seed 42).* Head only: 48.37, with *all* 10,000 predictions
positive. $r=1$ / 4 / 16 / 64: 80.03 / 82.52 / 83.23 / 83.86. The trainable
parameter counts are identical. On MPS the LoRA runs were bit-for-bit
repeatable; full fine-tuning gave 85.70 and 85.34 for two runs with the same
settings. The code and all the numbers are in the book's `Claude outputs/`
folder.
:::

### Reading the table

**Row 1 is the control, and it fails.** Freezing the encoder and training only
the classification head — 1,538 parameters — produces a model whose macro-F1 is
48.37 and whose accuracy is 93.68. Those are not new numbers. They are exactly
@sec-bake-off's majority-class baseline. A negative-class F1 of zero is consistent with a model
that has fallen back on the majority class, and in the re-run the prediction
counts confirmed it: it answered *positive* for all 10,000 test reviews. On a
corpus that is 93.68% positive that is a locally sensible thing to do. [A frozen encoder with a trainable head is a linear probe rather
than an adapter-based method, and on an imbalanced task it can collapse]{.hl} —
whether you file linear probes under "parameter-efficient fine-tuning" is a
naming question; what matters is that they change no representation. The F1 on
the negative class is 0.00. Discount this row by the learning-rate caveat
above: it was run at the shared rate. In the re-run, class weights in the loss
and a higher rate (1e-3 and 1e-2) lifted the probe to 63.85 and 64.90
macro-F1: better than 48.37, but more than 15 points behind the LoRA rows.
Exercise 1 is that experiment.

That row is in the table because the difference between it and the LoRA rows is
the entire argument. The linear probe trains only the final classification
head; LoRA here adds small adapters to the `query` and `value` projections of
every encoder block, so the gradient passes through the encoder. LoRA does not
train every weight or every module; it spreads its change inside the encoder,
across all blocks.

**In this run rank stops mattering quickly.** Going from $r=1$ to $r=8$ buys
2.2 macro-F1 points; from $r=8$ to $r=64$ — eight times the parameters — the
score goes from 82.69 to 82.39. That small difference comes from one run; it
does not show that the higher rank hurt. The re-run did not repeat that last
step either: over three seeds $r=1$ scored **80.55 ± 0.65** and $r=64$
**84.05 ± 0.26** ($r=8$ 82.66 on one seed), so in our runs rank kept giving small
gains at 2e-4. On the other hand, $r=8$ at its own validation-chosen rate
(1e-3) reached 83.68 ± 0.40 — tuning the rate bought as much as an eightfold
rank.

One confound in that row is worth naming, because it is the thing the
literature actually argues about. With $\alpha = 2r$ the effective scale
$\alpha/r$ is a constant 2 at every rank, so this sweep is *not* the disguised
scale sweep it would have been under a fixed $\alpha$. But holding $\alpha/r$
constant is itself a choice: @kalajdzievski2023rank shows that a
$\Theta(1/r)$ scaling makes gradients shrink as rank grows, and that stable
learning at high rank wants $\Theta(1/\sqrt{r})$ instead — with "higher rank
does not help" as the predicted symptom. But this single-seed curve does not
show that the $r=64$ result comes from that scaling alone; the learning rate
and the seed are confounders too. How much rank pays under the common
$\alpha = 2r$ rule, and what changes under rank-stabilised scaling, needs a
separate rate-and-scale sweep over several seeds; this chapter did not run it.

In the book's run the curve rises once and flattens; in the re-run it flattens
more slowly. What both share is that after $r=1$ the gain from rank is the same
size as, or smaller than, the effect of the learning rate. The low-rank
hypothesis in @sec-lora leads you to expect good results at small ranks, but it
does not by itself prove this task's curve; choose the rank over a few seeds on
validation score, memory and cost.

**The full fine-tune wins, and it wins on one class.** 83.90 against $r=8$'s
82.69 is a 1.21-point difference in this run, and the minority class is where
it comes from: F1(neg) 70.16 against 67.23, worth +2.93 points on that class.
It is not *all* of the story, though — back out the other half and the full
fine-tune is slightly *behind* on the majority class, F1(pos) 97.64 against
98.15. A 2.93-point gain on one class and a 0.51-point loss on the other
average to the 1.21 you see. But look at the accuracy column — [in this table every single LoRA run is *more* accurate
overall than the full fine-tune]{.hl} (96.09–96.58 against 95.62). On
imbalanced data the two metrics reward different trade-offs; how the decision
boundary moved, only per-class errors and the probability distribution can
show. In the re-run this split *did not repeat*: full fine-tuning (2e-5) also
led on accuracy — 96.83% against 96.60% for tuned LoRA $r=8$. The confusion
matrices (seed 42) show full fine-tuning catching more of the negative class
(415 against 382 of the 632 negatives) and making fewer errors overall (317
against 331). So the accuracy-versus-macro-F1 split in this table may be a
property of this setup rather than of LoRA in general. Which metric you want is
still a product decision, not a training one.

**Rank 1 is the result worth sitting with.** 38,402 trainable parameters —
36,864 in the adapters plus the 1,538-parameter head, 0.035% of the model, a
file you could email — take a frozen encoder from 48.37 to
80.47 macro-F1, clearing @sec-bake-off's tf-idf baseline by more than four
points (80.55 ± 0.65 in the re-run). A small adaptation capacity spread across
the layers can be enough for this task; that does not mean capacity plays no
role.

**The wall-clock column.** On this device and settings $r=8$ took 10m 04s and
the full fine-tune 11m 59s: about 1.19×. The 373× difference in trainable
parameters did not carry over to time. In the re-run (M5 Max) the ratio was
1.42× (6m 54s against 9m 47s), so the ratio depends on hardware and software.
A profile would show which operations set the time.

The head-only row shows something by contrast. It finishes in 3m 35s (3m 14s
in the re-run) — 3.3× faster than the full fine-tune — because with nothing
trainable inside the encoder, backpropagation never enters it. LoRA's adapters
sit inside the blocks; their gradients follow the computation path through the
encoder. Gradients for the frozen main weights are not kept, but the backward
pass does not go away. [In this setup LoRA bought memory and portability but
did not markedly shorten the backward pass]{.hl}; measure the speed-up on your
own model and implementation.

**And the memory column is where the chapter's arithmetic meets the floor.**
The 16-bytes-versus-2 table compared only selected parameter state; it did not
predict an eightfold cut in total peak memory. Measured, LoRA cuts it 1.40× —
6.07 GiB to 4.32 GiB. Subtract the resident parameters — 0.41 GiB, measured
before the first forward pass — from $r=8$'s 4.32 GiB peak and 3.91 GiB is left
over. [**Most of that is activations**]{.hl}, but not all of it: gradients,
workspace and temporary tensors are in there too, and without a detailed memory
profile we cannot split it. The choice of rank barely changes it. QLoRA's
authors measuring 567 MB of input gradients against 26 MB of adapter
parameters at 7B points the same way. The re-run also showed that *when* the
column is sampled matters: LoRA's 4.32 matches exactly a value taken at the
first forward pass, before any optimizer state exists; for full fine-tuning the
first forward pass held 3.82 GiB and later steps, with Adam state, 6.96 GiB (a
ratio of 1.61×).

Notice also that peak memory is essentially constant across ranks — 4.32 GiB at
$r=1$ and 4.37 GiB at $r=64$ (4.40 in the re-run) — for the same reason. And notice the
head-only row at 0.41 GiB: no backward pass through the encoder means no
retained activations, an order of magnitude less memory, and a model that does
not work.

### What the numbers do not show

Three honest caveats, because a lab that only produces good news is a
demonstration, not an experiment.

- **These ratios do not carry over to other scales.** The 1.40× memory ratio
  and the 1.19× speed-up (1.61× and 1.42× in the re-run) are laptop numbers at
  110M parameters with a batch of 32, where activations dominate. Parameter
  state varies with model size; activations and temporary memory with the
  number of layers, batch, sequence length and checkpointing; as models widen
  the balance often tips towards parameters. The 119.7 and 15.5 GiB given for
  8B are static-state estimates, not measured peaks. Do not quote this table's
  ratios as general claims about LoRA.
- **Peak memory is one number standing in for a distribution.** It is the
  largest live allocation seen across 30 steps of a fixed-shape batch. Real
  training has variable sequence lengths and therefore a memory profile with a
  tail, and the tail is what actually kills a run at 3 a.m. Treat the column as
  a comparison between rows, not as a provisioning figure.
- **One seed, one dataset, one language.** The table's runs are two-epoch runs
  on a single split, one seed per row. The 0.30 separating $r=8$ from $r=64$,
  and the 0.03 separating $r=1$ from $r=4$, are not enough to read a ranking
  into. The re-run's repeated seeds give the scale: the standard deviation
  across seeds within a row was 0.26–0.65 points, and on MPS full fine-tuning
  moved 0.36 points even with the same seed. At that scale the gap between row
  1 and everything else, and the 1.7 points between tuned full fine-tuning and
  LoRA, are above the noise; the accuracy-versus-macro-F1 split that the table
  shows for every LoRA row did not repeat in the re-run. (The parameter counts
  are the configuration's arithmetic, not measurements, so no seed can move
  them.)

### Your turn

1. **Reproduce row 1's collapse, then fix it.** Run the head-only baseline and
   confirm from the predicted class counts that you get the majority-class
   result. Now fix it *without* unfreezing anything: tune the learning rate and
   class weights in the loss (or resampling) on a validation slice. Report how
   close you get to the LoRA rows on the same test set, and discuss whether the
   gap is *consistent with* a change in representation; the training setups
   differ, so do not read an exact split off one experiment.
2. **Find the rank that stops paying.** Sweep $r \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\}$
   with three seeds each. Plot macro-F1 against $\log_2 r$ with error bars.
   State the rank at which the curve flattens, and — this is the part that
   matters — state whether your error bars can distinguish it from the rank
   below it.
3. **Break the $\alpha = 2r$ convention on purpose.** Fix $r = 8$ and sweep
   $\alpha \in \{2, 8, 16, 64\}$. Watch how the $\alpha/r$ scale from
   @sec-lora affects the loss, the gradients and the task score, and compare the
   effect with a learning-rate sweep; do not assume the two are exactly
   equivalent.
4. **Change what you attach to.** Keep $r = 8$ and move the adapters from
   `query, value` to the MLP (`intermediate.dense`, `output.dense`). Work out
   the new parameter count from @sec-lora's formula *before* you run it — the
   *adapter-only* count is 2.5× the `query, value` figure, and you should be
   able to say why the factor is 2.5 and not 2 (adding the head to the total
   trainable count changes the ratio). Compare scores under the same validation
   setup: does the score follow the parameters?
5. **Show the undo.** Keep the base checkpoint of the same revision. Fine-tune
   with LoRA, save the adapter, then load the base model and compare its
   weights to the original checkpoint tensor by tensor. Then count how many
   tensors differ in the task checkpoint after a full fine-tune, and show that
   reloading the saved base checkpoint undoes the full fine-tune too. Explain
   the operational difference from @sec-forgetting: it is not reversibility as
   such but managing the task update as a separate, small file.
6. **Measure your own forgetting.** Take your fine-tuned encoder and run the
   masked-language probe from @sec-forgetting on Turkish text from a domain
   neither you nor the fine-tune touched. Compare full fine-tuning against
   LoRA. Then mix 10% general Turkish into your fine-tuning set and measure
   again.
7. **Go where the baseline cannot follow.** @sec-bake-off's tf-idf model
   reached 76.21 macro-F1 with no GPU at all. Find an input where the
   fine-tuned model is right and tf-idf is wrong, and one where the reverse
   holds. The second is harder to find and more informative when you do.

**Deliverable:** one table with the same columns as ours, your own numbers in
it, and a paragraph that writes down your minimum macro-F1, negative-class F1,
latency and maintenance requirements and justifies the lowest *total-cost*
configuration that clears them. Keeping the tf-idf baseline is an option too;
if nothing clears the bar, say so and defer deployment.

## Intuition checks {#sec-post-training-intuition}

Answer before expanding. Every one of these is a place where a plausible mental
model of fine-tuning produces the wrong engineering decision.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. LoRA trains 0.035% of the weights. Does it use 0.035% of the memory, and run ~3,000× faster?

Neither, and the gap between those expectations and the measurements is the
most useful thing in this chapter.

On memory: freezing a parameter removes seven of its eight instalments —
optimizer state is three quarters of the training bill, the gradient an eighth,
the weight itself an eighth. So LoRA removes most of the *optimizer* memory,
but [what dominates at small model sizes is activations]{.hl}, and no choice of
rank touches those.

On speed: $r = 8$ trains **373× fewer parameters** and runs **1.19× faster**.
That is the whole speedup. LoRA saves optimizer work, and on a 110M model with
a batch of 32 there is not much optimizer work to save. The technique pays off
on large models and on serving many adapters, not on wall-clock for a small
fine-tune.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Freezing the encoder and training just the classifier head — is that parameter-efficient fine-tuning?

It is a linear probe rather than an adapter-based method — some people file
probes under the PEFT umbrella and some do not, so say which you mean. The
substantive difference is that a probe changes no representation, and on this
task, at the shared learning rate this lab used, it collapses completely.

Training 1,538 parameters on a frozen encoder produced macro-F1 **48.37** and
accuracy **93.68** — exactly @sec-bake-off's majority-class baseline, with F1 on
the negative class of **0.00**. The model learned to answer *positive* every
time.

[LoRA does not train a small *part* of the model; it trains a small number of
weights *throughout* it]{.hl}, and that distinction is the entire argument. Rank
1 — 38,402 trainable parameters, 0.035% of the model, a file you could email —
takes the same frozen encoder from 48.37 to **80.47**, clearing the tf-idf
baseline by four points.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Higher LoRA rank means more capacity. Should you use the highest rank you can afford?

No — the curve flattens almost immediately and then goes slightly backwards.

Measured: $r=1 \to r=8$ buys **2.2** macro-F1 points. $r=8 \to r=64$, eight
times the parameters, *loses* **0.30**. Stand on the flat part.

The caveat that makes this honest: 0.30 is the size of gap a single seed cannot
resolve, so do not read a ranking into it. What matters is the shape — [the
curve rises once and then stops]{.hl}. Rank is an afterthought on this task,
which is what the low-rank hypothesis in @sec-lora would lead you to expect.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. Your full fine-tune beats LoRA on macro-F1 but loses on accuracy. Which is broken?

Neither. You are looking at a product decision wearing the costume of a
training result.

Full fine-tuning scored 83.90 macro-F1 against $r=8$'s 82.69, and the minority
class is where the difference lives: F1(neg) 70.16 against 67.23, +2.93 points,
against a 0.51-point *loss* on the majority class (F1(pos) 97.64 against
98.15). But [every single LoRA
run is *more* accurate overall]{.hl} — 96.09–96.58 against 95.62.

Full fine-tuning had enough freedom to move the decision boundary toward the
negatives. Macro-F1 rewards that; plain accuracy punishes it. Which you want
depends on what a missed complaint costs relative to a false alarm, which is
@sec-classification-costs' question, and no training table can answer it for
you.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. A 65B model needs "more than 780 GB" to fine-tune. Where does that number come from?

$65 \times 10^9$ parameters × **12 bytes**. The instructive part is that the
paper does not say which twelve, and two readings both fit.

Reading one: the three fp32 rows — master weight, Adam's $m$, Adam's $v$ — with
the bf16 weight and gradient pushing the real figure to $65 \times 16 = 1{,}040$
GB, which is what "more than" absorbs. Reading two: bf16 weight, bf16 gradient,
fp32 $m$, fp32 $v$, no master copy, with "more than" absorbing activations
instead.

[Either decomposition lands on the same conclusion: the headline is dominated
by state that exists only because the parameter is being trained.]{.hl} Freeze
it and that state evaporates — which is the one-sentence case for PEFT.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. Your fine-tuned model got worse at things it used to do. What happened, and is it avoidable?

Catastrophic forgetting, and it is a *consequence* of the thing you wanted
rather than a bug you can patch out.

Gradient descent on a narrow objective moves weights that other capabilities
depended on. The mitigations are all versions of *move less*: lower learning
rate, fewer epochs, PEFT (the base weights cannot drift, although the merged
model can still forget, as @sec-forgetting measured), or mixing
some general data back into the fine-tuning set.

The reason this matters more than it sounds: [it is measured against whatever
you thought to evaluate]{.hl}. If your eval suite only covers the new task, the
model can lose a capability you never tested and you will ship it. Build the
regression suite before the fine-tune, not after.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-post-training-interview}

The questions below test when to choose a technique as much as how it works;
every answer has a measurement or a piece of arithmetic behind it.

::: {.column-margin}
A good signal in this area is a candidate who volunteers *when not to
fine-tune*. As in the decision tree (@sec-decision-tree), first pin down the
kind of error and a measurable quality bar; then compare prompting, retrieval
and adaptation.
:::

1. **What does fine-tuning actually fix, and what does it not?** It fixes
   *behaviour* — format, style, task framing, refusal patterns, domain register.
   It can teach chosen facts too, but for keeping current organisational
   knowledge reliable and citable, consider retrieval separately; a fact added by
   fine-tuning is expensive to update and hard to attribute. The framing that
   makes this land: a base model is not broken, it is answering a different
   question — given this text, what comes next. Fine-tuning teaches it which
   question you are asking; it does not reliably teach it new answers, and
   [when a team uses fine-tuning as its knowledge-update mechanism, it often
   disappoints]{.hl}. Then say the practical half: first test whether the error
   comes from knowledge, the prompt, the output schema or the model's ability,
   and choose the method accordingly.

2. **Explain LoRA to someone who knows linear algebra.** Freeze $W$ and learn
   $\Delta W = BA$ where $B$ is $d \times r$ and $A$ is $r \times k$ with $r \ll
   \min(d,k)$. Forward becomes $Wx + \frac{\alpha}{r}BAx$, and at serving time
   you can fold $\frac{\alpha}{r}BA$ into $W$, removing the separate adapter
   multiply. Two details that show you have used
   it: $A$ is randomly initialised and $B$ is zeroed, so the adapter starts as an
   exact no-op and training cannot destabilise the pretrained model at step 0;
   and $\alpha$ behaves *roughly* as a learning-rate multiplier on the adapter
   path, which
   is why $\alpha = 2r$ is a convention rather than a law.

3. **How much memory does fine-tuning need?** Decompose it rather than guessing.
   Per trainable parameter in a chosen mixed-precision Adam setup: bf16 weight 2,
   bf16 gradient 2, fp32 master weight 4, fp32 $m$ and $v$ 8 together — roughly
   16 bytes of static parameter state. Then name the term that decomposition
   omits and that often dominates at small scale: activations and temporary
   buffers, which vary with batch, sequence length and checkpointing and which
   freezing parameters does not much reduce (in the lab LoRA cut peak memory
   only 1.40×). That
   last sentence is what separates someone who has read about LoRA from someone
   who has watched it fail to fit.

4. **SFT or DPO, and why did preference tuning become a separate stage?**
   SFT teaches "here is a good answer" from one target per prompt. It cannot
   express *this answer is better than that one*, and for qualities like
   helpfulness or tone the judgement is comparative — which is exactly why
   preference optimization exists as a separate stage. DPO's contribution is
   showing you can optimise the KL-regularized preference objective without
   training a separate reward network: [in that objective the reward can be
   expressed as the policy/reference log-ratio]{.hl} [@rafailov2023dpo].
   Practical note worth adding: an SFT start gives data–reference match in most
   recipes; DPO on a base model is mathematically defined, but it often
   disappoints when the preference data come from an instruction-following
   model.

5. **When would you *not* fine-tune?** When a simpler prompt, schema or
   reliable retrieval solves the measured problem; when you lack enough clean
   training and evaluation data; when the target behaviour will change often;
   when maintenance and regression costs outweigh the gain; or when you cannot
   build a regression suite for what you might break. Add the deployment
   argument: serving adapters cuts storage and the number of copies — but
   measure routing, versioning and concurrency costs too.

6. **You fine-tuned and the score got worse. How do you debug it?** First check
   the data split, the label distribution and that the evaluation code is
   correct. Then check the chat template
   — training with the wrong one teaches a format the server will never send;
   check whether the model collapsed to the majority class, which on an
   imbalanced task looks like a plausible accuracy (ours read 93.68% while
   scoring 0.00 F1 on the minority class); check the learning rate, since too
   high destroys pretrained structure and too low does nothing; and check
   whether your eval moved at all, because a frozen number usually means the
   trainable parameters were not the ones you thought. These are possible
   causes; test the learning rate and class balance in separate validation
   experiments rather than pinning one symptom on one cause.

## Where to go deeper

Read one thing before any paper: open a chat model's tokenizer and print
`tokenizer.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False)` for a two-turn
conversation. Checking the role and end-of-turn markers helps catch a
training–serving template mismatch early, and it takes a few seconds.


| resource | what it is |
|:--|:--|
| [Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI) — Andrej Karpathy | three hours covering pretraining through RLHF; the clearest available account of where each training stage's behaviour comes from |
| [`trl`](https://github.com/huggingface/trl) | SFT, DPO and PPO in one library, with readable trainers — the fastest way to see what each objective actually optimises |
| [`peft`](https://github.com/huggingface/peft) | LoRA and its relatives; the source is short enough to read and settles what rank actually changes |
| [Interconnects](https://www.interconnects.ai/) — Nathan Lambert | ongoing, well-sourced writing on post-training from someone who publishes open recipes |
| [Lil'Log on reward hacking](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2024-11-28-reward-hacking/) | the failure mode that every preference-optimisation method inherits, surveyed properly |

## Exercises

1. Print `apply_chat_template` for a two-turn conversation on two different
   model families. List every token that differs. Then explain, in terms of
   what SFT actually optimizes, why serving with family A's template a model
   trained with family B's degrades quality without raising an error.
2. Reproduce the example from @sec-sft with Llama 3's tokenizer: 31 tokens, 4
   of them the answer. Write out the `labels` tensor for both the masked and
   unmasked choice, and compute, for each, what fraction of the loss terms
   comes from prompt and template positions; do not mistake that share for
   gradient magnitude. Then run a short pilot with each mask and compare the
   answering behaviour on the same prompts.
3. @sec-lora gives two *possible* decompositions of QLoRA's ">780 GB" that both
   come to 12 bytes per parameter. Separate the memory items the paper reports
   from those it does not, and say what evidence you would need to choose
   between them. Then compute a conditional total for 8-bit Adam ($m$ and $v$
   in one byte each), listing the weight, gradient, master copy, moments and
   scaling metadata you assume; state the new ratio between a trained and a
   frozen parameter and one thing the reduced precision could plausibly cost
   you. Do not present the result as real peak memory.
4. Open the `config.json` of a model not in @sec-lora's table and check the
   input/output sizes of the actual target `Linear` modules (`head_dim`, gated
   MLPs and module names vary by model). Compute the *adapter-only* parameter
   count for LoRA $r=16$ on (a) `q_proj, v_proj` and (b) attention + MLP. Then
   load the model with `peft` and compare with the total trainable count;
   verify the source of any difference (biases, a classifier head or other
   modules left trainable) in the model.
5. LoRA initialises $A$ random and $B$ zero. Work out what happens for $A$
   zero and $B$ random: write down $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A$ and
   $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial B$ at step 0 (state the non-zero input and
   upstream-gradient assumption) and say whether the run escapes. Two of the
   four combinations start exactly at the pretrained model *and* generally have
   a non-zero gradient — identify them and say what the gradients have in
   common. Then propose an experiment that tests whether the same starting
   output guarantees the same training trajectory.
6. A team says their model "gives wrong prices for our products" and asks for
   a fine-tune. Walk them down @sec-decision-tree, out loud, in five sentences.
   Then construct the variant of their complaint for which fine-tuning *is* the
   right answer, and say what data it would need.
7. You have 4,000 prompts, one written answer each, and a complaint that the
   model "is too verbose and too eager to agree". Decide between more SFT and
   DPO. Say exactly what you would collect for each, how many items, and how
   you would know within a week whether it worked.
8. A colleague explains a disappointing DPO run on a base model with "the model
   does not answer yet, so there is nothing to rank". Look at
   $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}$: does the loss generate new answers during
   training, and what does it hold fixed? Explain the role of the reference
   log-probabilities. Then design an experiment that compares a base model and
   an SFT model on the same preference pairs, measuring data coverage and
   evaluation results; do not assume the failure or its cause before
   measuring.
9. GRPO replaces the value model with the mean reward of $G$ samples from the
   same prompt. Under independent samples the group mean has variance
   $\operatorname{Var}(r)/G$. Taking a learned value estimator's error variance
   and bias into account too, discuss which estimator would have the lower
   mean squared error; if the samples are not independent, say how correlation
   changes this. Then describe a task where the group mean would be the worse
   baseline.
10. Design the forgetting evaluation you would actually run for a Turkish
    customer-support fine-tune. Name the benchmark, say why it is the right
    one, and state the threshold at which you would refuse to ship. Then
    explain why the threshold has to be written down before you see the
    fine-tuned model's results.
